title: Ops risk heatmap: cloud-managed vs dedicated inference
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is a lightweight operational risk heatmap and messaging brief for field-facing GTM and solutions teams. Audience: platform architects, SRE leads, procurement evaluation committees. Goal: give a concise, demo-friendly framing of where cloud-managed (AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoints) vs dedicated/reserved inference (Redwood Dedicated / Private) create different operational risk profiles and where Redwood’s win themes should land.

Summary headline (one-liner):
Cloud-managed endpoints are fast to try; dedicated inference is faster to trust in production. We position Redwood as the bridge that keeps developer velocity while reducing long‑tail operational risk (latency spikes, noisy neighbors, compliance gaps).

How to use this doc:
- Run as a 10-minute primer before customer technical deepdives.
- Use the heatmap to map customer priorities (latency SLOs, data residency, cost predictability, failover guarantees).
- Pull the sample rebuttals and demo ideas into deal-specific playbooks.

Heatmap axes (operational impact vs likelihood) - short form notes:
- Latency tail risk: High impact / Medium likelihood for cloud-managed. Noise from multi-tenant endpoints, cross-region fallbacks, cold starts. For Dedicated: Low impact / Low likelihood (guaranteed shards, reserved capacity).
- Cost volatility: High impact / High likelihood on hyperscalers when bursty workloads or token spikes occur (eg. model updates or evaluation loops). Dedicated: Medium impact / Medium likelihood (committed cost but predictable unit economics).
- Data control & residency: High impact / Medium likelihood for customers in regulated industries. Hyperscalers: control plane and logs often traverse vendor-managed services; private deployments reduce audit surface.
- Operational troubleshooting: Medium impact / High likelihood with cloud-managed endpoints due to opaque scheduling and multi-layered vendor telemetry. Dedicated: Low impact / Medium likelihood — more surface area but clearer ownership.
- Security & key management: Medium impact / Medium likelihood. Hyperscalers provide KMS but customers sometimes need dedicated HSM/KMS integration and stricter audit chains (Redwood Private).
- Rollback and model governance: High impact / Low-to-Medium likelihood. Managed endpoints may lag in model versioning and can force coupling of model upgrades and infra changes. Redwood’s rollout primitives (canary, A/B, automatic fallback) are a win.

Top win themes to emphasize (message snippets for demos/emails):
1) Predictable economics without sacrificing latency: "Committed pools for predictable p99s and per-token economics that you can model."
2) Control plane locality and auditability: "Keep control plane actions in your VPC and tie every inference to a customer-controlled audit trail."
3) Graceful degradation and fallback: "If a peak or region outage occurs, Redwood will route to cheaper compatible model variants or fall back to cached responses — keeping customers online."
4) Developer ergonomics + Ops controls: "Same API surface from sandbox to private, with operational knobs exposed for SLOs and cost guardrails."
5) Quantization and batching guidance: "We recommend config profiles per workload; we measure cost/quality tradeoffs so you don’t guess."

Common customer priorities we map to pain + Redwood counterpoints:
- Priority: Consistent p99 < 200ms for user-facing chat
  Pain: Managed endpoints hit noisy neighbor issues during business hours
  Redwood counterpoint: Dedicated pools with autoscale policies and KV caching to preserve p99s.

- Priority: Auditable data flows for auditors
  Pain: Vendor control plane logs, third-party telemetry
  Redwood counterpoint: Private deployment option, customer-managed KMS/HSM, exportable audit logs.

- Priority: Predictable monthly cost for forecasting and procurement
  Pain: Per-token bills vary wildly with burst workloads and batch evals
  Redwood counterpoint: Reserved capacity offers predictable commits + burst buffers and cost-per-token modelling.

Objections (field-ready) and rebuttals:
- "Hyperscalers give us the fastest path and we don’t want to manage infra."
  Rebuttal: "True for proofs-of-concept. For production SLOs and procurement, teams inevitably hit runbooks, incident playbooks, and cost surprises. Redwood removes much of that by providing reserved pools and control-plane locality without rewriting your app code."

- "Why not just use provider KMS and logging?"
  Rebuttal: "Provider KMS is fine for many cases; for regulated workloads customers need HSM-level attestations and retention controls that require customer-run components — we integrate both models and make migration smoother than a full rewrite."

- "Isn’t vendor lock-in a risk with Redwood Dedicated?"
  Rebuttal: "We expose the same API surface as our hosted offering and support model portability via standard formats and model catalog versioning; the most common lock-in is app-level prompts/inputs, not the serving runtime."

Suggested demo flows (15–25 minutes each) - order matters:
1) Latency incident replay (15 mins): show a simulated noisy neighbor in managed endpoint, then failover to Redwood Dedicated pool with preserved p99. Visualize token cost delta, p99 graphs, and a one-click rollback.
2) Compliance walkthrough (20 mins): show audit log export, KMS integration, and a canary rollout inside a VPC. Include sample SOC2 checklist items.
3) Cost predictability lab (20 mins): take a real token workload (chat + embeddings), show hyperscaler bill shock with spikes, then show reserved capacity math and how batching/quantization reduces unit cost.

Decision anchors and metrics to surface in every deal:
- p50/p95/p99 latency comparisons across peak windows
- cost per 1M tokens under baseline and peak scenarios
- time-to-recover (TTR) for region/zone failure simulated
- audit log chain length / retention windows / export time
- policy: number of policy knobs (canary %, fallback targets, quantization profile count)

Battle-card snippets for AE/SE quick reference:
- Lead with customer priority (latency vs cost vs compliance) — pick the right anchor
- If latency is primary: demo latency incident replay + p99 numbers up front
- If compliance is primary: demo VPC/KMS/HSM + audit export flow
- If cost is primary: show reserved vs on-demand math and quantization suggestions

Partner/companion collateral suggestions:
- Short one-pager: "Production inference decision checklist" (two pages, checklist + quick scoring rubric)
- Notebook: "Quick cost calibration" (Jupyter with sample workload and cost model)
- Demo video (3–5 min): latency incident replay clip + narrated callouts

Open questions & next steps for GTM ops:
- Validate p99 SLO targets with field SREs at 3 reference accounts (ask SEs to collect traces).
- Build a 5-minute latency incident replay automation for demos (capture, inject noise, failover).
- Produce an audit checklist template mapped to SOC2/ISO items for regulated customers.

Notes / caveats (internal):
- Avoid naming specific hyperscaler bugs or making claims about outages beyond public incidents; frame as "multi-tenant tail risk" not vendor blame.
- This doc is deliberately ops-centric. For executive briefs, compress to 3 bullets: velocity, predictability, control.

Appendix: quick scripting hooks for demos (SE cheat-sheet)
- Canary policy example: canary=5%, ramp=30m, fallback=compatible-smaller-model
- Simulated noise: background request generator + artificial quantization mismatch to create KV cache misses
- Cost calc quick formula: committed_unit_cost = (monthly_commit / expected_tokens) + burst_buffer_markup

End of doc.
Feedback requests: please add any missing SRE personas we should loop into validation (pager rotations, oncall playbooks, compliance reviewers).
